items.text: Bumped the mod version to **2.0.1**.
New module: **SkipTutorial** — skips the vanilla first-time tutorial hints.
**AFKNotifier**: documents the `@afknotify <words>` route for custom nicknames.
**ItemSearch**: improved command/autocomplete guidance.

**Confetti on Advancement is an actual celebration now.** The burst was ~40 dust particles at scale 0.7-1.3 in a single uniform spread — close to invisible in daylight. It now opens with a centre pop, splits into three bands (fast outward ring, slow drift, and a fountain that arcs and falls), doubles the dust scale to 1.2-2.4, and trails `FIREWORK` shimmer behind the confetti. Default count 40 → 120, ceiling 200 → 600. Applied to **both** copies of `FireworksFx` (`src/main/java` and the `mc26_3` override) so 26.3 does not keep the old effect.

**StructureNotifier no longer fails silently.** Its detection wrapped everything in an empty `catch (Exception) {}`, so a mapping change or a throwing registry lookup looked identical to "you are not inside a structure". Failures are now logged once per session, and a new **Debug Log** setting reports how many structure starts each chunk actually carries — which is the real question, since a multiplayer server does not send structure starts to clients at all.

**The "Redo onboarding" button no longer lies.** Its handler called `toast()` unconditionally after firing the bridge request, so it reported "First-run setup will run again on the next launch" even when Beacon refused the reset. The message is now the request's success notice, which only fires on an `ok` response; a failure surfaces the bridge's own error instead. Covered by a jsdom regression test that mocks the bridge in both states.

**Build fix:** `AFKFisher` referenced `FishingBobberEntity`, which does not exist in these mappings — the class is `net.minecraft.world.entity.projectile.FishingHook` (see `FishingHookAccessor`). All four references corrected; the code never compiled as shipped.

**CompactMessages actually collapses duplicates now.** The mixin fetched the module, tested `isEnabled()` and then had an *empty* `if` body, so `maxCombo()`/`counterColor()` were never called and enabling the module changed nothing — the only collapsing came from BetterChat's separate anti-spam. CompactMessages owns its duplicate detection now and appends a coloured `x N` badge, capped by **Max Combo**. New **Scan Depth** and **Ignore Timestamps** settings.

**BetterTab no longer covers the screen.** `TabListPlusMixin` rewrote *every* `13`, `11` and `9` in `PlayerTabOverlay.extractRenderState` to `40` to make room for numeric latency — but those literals are row metrics and padding, so the whole tab list inflated several times over. The wide layout is now opt-in via **Wide Ping Column** (off by default).

**SoundMuter's mute no longer sticks.** Enabling it used to walk the entire sound registry and `stop()` every matching identifier, killing portal/beacon hums mid-loop that nothing ever restarted — so disabling could not bring them back. Muting is preventive only now: the mixin rejects new matching plays, and disabling takes effect immediately with no state to undo.

**ItemSearch is reachable.** It only accepted `@search <item>` while every other module answers to `@ModuleName ...`, so the conventional `@ItemSearch wood` returned "Unknown setting/subcommand", and its only setting was the toggle keybind. Modules can now handle their own subcommands (`Module.onCommand`), ItemSearch takes `@ItemSearch <item>`, and it gains **Scope** and **Show Slots** settings.

**AFK Fisher:** the description no longer credits Meteor, the bite `pling` is gone (with the now-meaningless Bite Alert setting), and a catch is counted once per bobber instead of once per catch path — the "Caught N fish" tally was inflated.

**"Redo onboarding on next launch" no longer silently drops the wizard.** The flags really were being cleared and reloaded; the launch check was the problem. `Onboarding.onClientTick` set `armed = false` *before* attempting to open the page, so if that one open failed the setup was dropped for the whole launch with nothing logged. The retry budget now covers both waits (Chromium downloading, and browser-registered-but-won't-take-the-page), the setup only disarms once the page actually opened, and every branch logs — so the next launch's log says exactly whether the reset was written or the show path failed.
Regenerated the module catalogue: it had drifted to 55 modules/232 settings while the Java registry held 56/234 before any of the above.
Bumped the mod version to **2.0.0-prerelease**.
The first-run **Chromium install now shows a real progress bar** (with a percentage) on the loading screen, driven by the download's own byte-level progress instead of an endless spinner.
The **3D boot intro now preloads before it plays**: the first frames — which compile every shader — are drawn invisibly, so the opening no longer hitches.

The screen **stays black through the whole handoff** from the Chromium install to the boot intro: the loading screen paints an opaque black frame (no blurred menu underneath) and the wizard's first paint is black, so there is no white flash or menu glimpse.

The finished **3D beacon now stays on as a live backdrop** for the whole onboarding: after the cinematic it settles on the beacon's hero frame and idles in a slow, cheap orbit behind the frosted wizard, and the old flat "transparent logo" welcome card is gone (the PNG only returns as a fallback when WebGL is unavailable).

**Themes got a real art pass** (Spicetify-style): each theme gains a two-colour nebula glow and a soft vignette behind the glass, the theme picker swatches now preview each sky (glows + star specks), and *Starry Night* reads like a proper indigo night with a purple nebula.

The theme/accent chosen in first-run onboarding now **forwards to the main app**: the client stores them as `uiTheme`/`accent` and the app reads them back on launch (and pushes its own changes back over the bridge), so the look no longer snaps back to a default.
The top-right **Beacon corner logo expands on hover to show the running version**, and it now also sits on the main menu even before the first-run setup has been completed.

The **first-run setup now paints an opaque black backdrop** for its whole lifetime, so the blurred menu/panorama no longer shows through in the stretch between the install screen and the 3D intro (the app keeps its transparent, world-showing backdrop).
The standalone **"BEACON" wordmark** over the intro is gone; the welcome reads *"Welcome to Beacon"* only.

**Performance pass for the software (SwiftShader) renderer** the embedded browser uses: the idle backdrop drops to a lower resolution/24 fps, the cinematic drops MSAA, and the always-on animated atmosphere no longer runs full-screen `filter: blur()` (the two big glows are unblurred radial gradients; Mist/Aurora particle blurs are much lighter) — smoother intro and faster menu opens.
The intro's hidden **warm-up now pre-renders a spread of timeline frames** instead of just the opening frame, so the shader compile no longer stalls the start and the mid-intro energy merge.

The intro's **soundtrack now starts with the first visible frame** rather than at mount: it used to run a second or so ahead of the picture during the hidden warm-up, and the opening then snapped forward to catch up — the stall-and-jump at the start.

Opening the app **straight after the first-run setup no longer flashes the wizard's 3D backdrop**: one browser serves both pages, so the outgoing page is cleared off the surface before the new one is navigated to.

**Typing in the app's search no longer rebuilds the menu.** Only the module boxes that stop matching are hidden and the ones that start matching again are revealed, so the page stops fading out and re-animating on every keystroke.
The **`⌘ K` hint box is gone** from the search bar.
The **GUI key (`K` by default) now also opens Beacon from the main menu**, not just in-game — module keybinds still win if one of them is bound to the same key.

**"Redo onboarding on next launch" actually replays the whole first run again.** It cleared `onboardingSeen` but not `introSeen`, and the page gates the 3D cinematic on the second flag — so the wizard came back with no intro at all, which is what made the button look dead.

The wizard's **Finish step and its confirmation now both say which key opens Beacon**, as a key chip rather than a line of small print. It quotes the key Beacon actually reports (`guiKeyLabel`), so it stays correct after a rebind, and the confirmation's version is large because that screen closes itself after ~2.5 s.

**Interface sounds** are now real: the app plays subtle click/navigation feedback (opt-in via Settings → Interface sounds), and the first-run wizard uses a fuller sting set (page turns, selection, a completion chime).
The mod **author is now "International Duck Incorporated"**, and Settings gains a **"Redo onboarding on next launch"** button that re-runs the first-run wizard (and 3D intro) on the next boot.
Extracted the built-in **Bagely** module into the standalone **Bagley** Fabric addon. Beacon no longer ships AI endpoint, memory, screenshot, or Bagley-specific platform code.
Added addon-safe incoming/outgoing chat observation events, generic settings-drawer actions, and module configuration aliases.

Existing `Bagely` enabled state, settings, and favourites are read as `Bagley` when the addon is installed. The addon migrates its private `beacon-bagely…` files to Bagley names without logging credentials.

Added the addon API and player migration guides. The Bagley source tree is published separately for GitLab. All notable changes to Beacon are documented in this file, in the [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) format. Per-version notes for older releases (0.2.1 through 1.8.17) remain in [`releases/`](releases/) as a historical record; this file is the changelog going forward.

**The first-run onboarding intro is now a real 3D cinematic.** `webui/onboarding.html` opens on a fullscreen WebGL scene that renders the Minecraft beacon from `assets/models/beacon.glb` — the centrepiece, `GLBConverted`, CC-BY-4.0 by owencroft0, attributed in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`. Blue energy bands and motes arrive from off-screen, spiral in on a drifting helix, are pulled through the beacon's glass and absorbed at a target measured from the model's own geometry, and then the beacon activates: core emissive, a short flash, a shockwave, UnrealBloom and a Minecraft-style beam, while the camera pushes in for the absorption and opens up for the reveal. The reference clip was used as the **audio** reference only (it is never rendered): its audio track is the intro's soundtrack, its ~1.1 s of leading silence is skipped, and its measured beats drive the cue table — `webui/generate_intro_cues.py` re-measures the clip with ffmpeg and writes `assets/audio/beacon-intro.cues.json`, which `webui/intro3d_verify.py` cross-checks against the module. The whole cinematic is one pure function of a single visual time (`webui/assets/vendor/intro3d-timeline.js`) with `INTRO_START → … → COMPLETE` states, so it is deterministic, seekable, frame-rate independent and tunable in one table. Rendering never waits on audio: if autoplay is refused the scene still initialises, animates and finishes, and the first tap starts the sound without skipping the shot (`Esc` or the Skip button skips). Every failure — no WebGL, missing module, missing/broken model, failed init, a stall — disposes the scene and hands the screen to the existing onboarding welcome screen, and the intro is never allowed to block onboarding. three.js r180 and the post-processing addons are vendored locally under `webui/assets/vendor/` (no CDN), with the rationale in `webui/INTRO3D.md` and `webui/assets/vendor/README.md`.

**First-run onboarding, wired up.** `webui/onboarding.html` is now packaged as `assets/beacon/webui/onboarding.html` and opens automatically on the first launch once the HTML UI is ready: it shows at the main menu, never over a game in progress, and stays pending if Chromium is unavailable so it is not silently consumed. `@onboarding` (alias `@setup`) re-opens it at any time, which is how the page is re-tested without deleting `beacon.json`. Finishing — or skipping — posts `onboarding.complete` over the typed bridge and persists the theme, accent, sound toggle, sound volume and favourite modules into `beacon.json` (`uiTheme`, `accent`, `soundVolume`, `onboardingSeen`); favourite ids that match no loaded module are dropped instead of being saved as favourites that could never resolve. The same values are exposed to the UI through the bridge snapshot's `preferences`.

**Bagley follow-up conversations with an LLM-controlled stop.** After a reply, the same requester can continue without repeating Bagley's name for a bounded window (default 45 seconds). The model itself decides when the conversation is over: a new `no_response` tool call (or the `[[bagley_no_reply]]` marker on endpoints without function support) sends no public chat **and immediately ends the listening session**, so chat addressed to other players stops triggering Bagley instead of restarting the timer. A marker returned with surrounding text is now treated as a no-reply instead of publishing the model's commentary, follow-up sessions are hard-capped at five consecutive replies, and decision turns never post the public failure apology.

**Bagley nearby-entities and Baritone tools.** `get_nearby_entities` shares loaded entities within a requested radius (default 32, max 128 blocks). With **Allow Baritone actions (ban risk)** enabled, `baritone_go_to`/`baritone_stop` let the model navigate via the installed Baritone mod's `#goto`/`#stop` commands — advertised only when the mod is actually installed, with the model instructed to navigate only to player-provided coordinates. Both were previously stranded in the `Beacon-complete-7700335-…` bundle and never reached the compiled source, which is why the AI never used Baritone; they now build from `src/` for all Minecraft targets.

**HUD visibility modules.** **HideScoreboard** now provides independent, default-on controls for the sidebar scoreboard and on-screen chat feed. **HidePumpkinOverlay** is a separate Render module. Both update their render paths directly without forcing a chunk/world renderer rebuild, and legacy `HideOverlays` configuration is migrated.

**The 3D onboarding intro could never actually run in a build.** Beacon's loopback origin sent `connect-src 'none'` in its Content-Security-Policy, and three.js downloads `beacon.glb` with `fetch()` — which is what that directive governs, not `media-src` or `script-src`. Chromium therefore refused the model request before it left the browser, `GLTFLoader` reported a failure and the cinematic skipped straight to the welcome screen. The development harness never showed it because `python -m http.server` sends no CSP at all. The policy now allows `connect-src 'self'` (still nothing off-origin, the page never talks to the Internet), the model and soundtrack are served as `model/gltf-binary` and `audio/mpeg` instead of `application/octet-stream` (every response also carries `nosniff`), and `intro3d_verify.py` gained a section that checks the packaged origin instead of only the page.

**HTML UI console output now reaches the game log.** Page-side warnings and errors — including `[Beacon] 3D boot intro unavailable (<reason>)` and Chromium's own blocked-subresource reports — are forwarded as `[Beacon][HTML UI] …`, so a page that degrades no longer leaves the log silent about why.

**The intro's beacon is textured again — it is no longer a bare grey cube.** `beacon.glb` stores its three textures in bufferViews; `GLTFLoader` turns each one into a `blob:` URL and downloads it through `fetch()`. `connect-src 'self'` does not match `blob:` URLs even though the page created them, so the texture fetches were refused and the model rendered untextured. The served policy now allows `blob:` in both `connect-src` and `img-src` (`blob:` URLs inherit the page's origin and can only be created by it, so no new target is reachable). Verified against real Chromium: with the old policy the three texture fetches are CSP-refused and the shot is a plain cube; with the fix they succeed and the textured beacon renders.

**The boot cinematic (and its audio) no longer replays on every launch.** The page kept the "seen" flag only in `localStorage`, but the loopback origin is a fresh random port and token on every launch, so the store was empty each time. `onboarding.intro-seen` — which the page already posts but the bridge previously rejected as unknown — now persists a durable `introSeen` flag in `beacon.json`, the state snapshot exposes it, and the page asks for the snapshot before deciding whether to play (with a short fallback so a dead bridge cannot strand the player). `@onboarding` still opens the wizard, but the intro plays only once; `#replay` (or `?replay=1` when testing standalone) forces it again.

**Fullbright no longer unloads the visible map.** Gamma and Potion modes never touch chunk meshes. Entering, changing, or leaving Luminance mode now marks visible-range sections dirty and lets the normal compiler replace them while their old meshes stay on screen, instead of releasing every render buffer up front.

**SoundMuter applies immediately.** Enabling the module or any mute filter now stops matching sounds that are already playing through the public per-identifier sound-manager API; future matching sounds remain blocked by the play hook. Unrelated effects and music are left running, and rejoining is no longer required.

**Bagley provider, tool, passive-listener, follow-up, retry, failure reply, memory, nickname, and complete-answer controls.** Bagley now has Click GUI controls for provider profile, provider-appropriate reasoning effort, observation tools (tab list, nearby entities, and one current-game screenshot), an explicit ban-risk Baritone-navigation opt-in, client-only tool/loading notices, an opt-in five-second passive-listener decision window, natural same-requester follow-up questions with no-reply decisions, retries, the initial retry-delay seconds (default exponential waits: 5, 10, then 20 seconds), public exhausted-retry replies, busy notices, response token budget, reply detail, response audience, bounded local conversation memory, and protected long-term notes. The default disabled reasoning setting sends `reasoning_effort: none` to Ollama/OpenAI-compatible endpoints, fixing Qwen3 responses that otherwise contain only hidden thinking and no final `message.content`; OpenRouter instead receives its own excluded structured reasoning object. Tool screenshots are downscaled, attached only to the configured endpoint for a mention-triggered tool call, visibly announced only to the client, deleted locally immediately, and cleanly fall back if a non-vision endpoint returns HTTP 400. Passive windows never enter Bagley memory. Bagley now repairs missing/invalid config schema fields and backs up malformed JSON before recreating a usable local config. OpenRouter-style length-limited output is retried instead of being posted mid-sentence. Its private configuration also supports case-insensitive nickname triggers (including `Bags` by default). Memory and durable notes are stored separately in `beacon-bagley-memory.json`, and all maintained Minecraft overlays provide the failure toast.

**Minecraft 26.3 input target by default.** A plain Gradle build now selects the 26.3 overlay, including its SDL keyboard and mouse translation, instead of building a 26.2 jar whose GLFW-style input codes make the Click GUI appear unresponsive on 26.3. Older versions remain available through `-Pmc=<version>`.

**The build never worked.** The committed scaffold could not even configure: it used the pre-26.1 remapping plugin (`fabric-loom` 1.16.2, a combination that does not exist for the new plugin id) with `modImplementation` configurations that no longer exist. Now: `net.fabricmc.fabric-loom` 1.17-SNAPSHOT + plain `implementation`, per the canonical 26.2 template. `./gradlew build` is green for the first time in the repository's history.
Chat autocomplete cast every suggestion `String` to `java.lang.invoke.CallSite` — compiled fine, ClassCastException the moment the `@` menu opened.
`@search` set the ItemSearch query without lowercasing it (unlike the module's own chat path), so uppercase queries silently matched nothing.

FreecamCoreTest's epsilon was always-red against the shipped float-radian math; BeaconConfigTest still called a stale `EnabledModules.unknown` signature and could not compile against the current tree.
The Click GUI HTML prototype (`docs/beacon-ui.html`) and its two dedicated checkers — a second implementation of the GUI that only existed to be kept in sync. See `docs/CLICK-GUI-HTML-REMOVAL.md`.

The `@theme` command: it tried to set a `BeaconUI.currentTheme` field that has never existed on the Java GUI and could only ever fail. Runtime theming does not exist (the palette is compile-time constants); when it does, the command can return with a real implementation behind it.
The stale `deal ` autocomplete candidate left over from the AH Deal Sniper removal.

Prepared Beacon for multi-version Fabric builds from **Minecraft 1.21.11** through **26.3**: target matrix, per-target build directories, metadata/resource smoke checks, and compile-ready release artifacts.

**De-decompiled** (~1,200 lines of CFR artifacts removed): banners, redundant casts, `void x = …` eaten declarations, labeled blocks, swallowed mixin `(Object)` bridges, eaten string literals (logger names, texture identifiers, button labels), and a dozen genericity repairs.

**Zero runtime reflection** (~850 lines removed): EnderChestCapture (which reflected its *own* jar), ItemDraw, ReconnectFx, BookTools extraction, UiText, TabListFx and the pasteToBook/copyHeldBook/query field probes are all typed now, javap-verified against the 26.2 jar.
Chat branding centralised in `net.beacon.utils.BeaconText` (one prefix util instead of five ad-hoc `§`-literal shapes per module).
`ModuleManager` lookups are O(1) (concurrent class/name indexes; the ordered list stays the source of truth, with a subclass-safe fallback).
`EventBus.subscribe` takes an optional priority: higher runs first, equal priorities keep registration order.
CI on every push (hygiene gate → target metadata smoke checks → compile-ready tests/build) and automated tag releases with checksums.

**Bagley** — an opt-in, OpenAI Chat Completions-compatible assistant that replies in public chat when someone says `Bagley`. It sends only the triggering message and keeps endpoint credentials in the separate, non-shareable `config/beacon-bagley.json`; see the standalone [Bagley repository](https://gitlab.com/international-duck-incorporated/Bagley).
`Setting.visibleIf(guard, test)` — settings can declare they only make sense while another setting's value passes a predicate; the GUI honours it in render, hit-testing and height.
Config share codes: `@config export` / `@config import <code>` — the whole `beacon.json` as one pasteable string (gzip + URL-safe base64).
Keybind-conflict detection: conflicts are announced at config load and listed by `@binds`, because the losing module in a key clash just silently never fires.
`@bug` — a clickable link to a GitLab issue form prefilled from the Bug.md template (versions, OS, reproduce/expect skeleton).
JUnit 5 test suite (41 tests) wired into `./gradlew test`, replacing the two hand-run javac harnesses; `tools/verify/check_hygiene.py` gates the de-decompile/de-reflect invariants in CI.
See [`releases/`](releases/) — one file per version, kept as a historical record.

New movement module `no-slow`: decides for itself how much the item in use slows you down. 26.2 keeps the slowdown on the item itself - the `USE_EFFECTS` data component, read through one seam the client consults every tick it is eating, drinking, drawing or blocking - and the new `LocalPlayerUseSlowMixin` hands that decision to `NoSlowRules`, a pure decision table covered by `UseSlowRulesTest`. Ported from Raven B4's `NoSlow` with the same filter set (sword-only, disable-bow, disable-potions with thrown potions still overridable) and its one-way range: the slider only ever moves the multiplier up from vanilla's 0.2, and the default of 80% is exact vanilla parity. The description states the cost the way the desync family's does: a simulating server predicts 0.2, so the useful range is the server's to allow, not the module's.

New combat module `keep-sprint`: softens the price your own swings charge you. Vanilla multiplies the attacker's horizontal motion by 0.6 and drops sprint after every hit; `AttackEntityEvent` captures the motion going into the swing - the only moment the un-punished motion exists - and a tail mixin on `Player.attack` puts it back scaled by the slider, sprint re-raised. The default 40% restores exact vanilla motion, which makes the module's real function the kept sprint; the one-way range is Raven's, and the original's stop-sprint toggle is replaced by an explicit keep-sprint switch, since the knockback-module plumbing it served has no counterpart here. Two new mixins (`LocalPlayerUseSlowMixin`, `PlayerAttackMixin`) bring the config to nine entries and the per-class load guard covers them. Both descriptions carry the same honesty as the desync family: on Grim these are Simulation flags by design, on non-simulating servers they are free.

New network module `fake-lag`: holds the connection's own packets for a configurable delay - outbound (everything you send), inbound (everything the server sends), or both - releasing by age with hard flushes on teleport, damage and disconnect. Ported from Raven B4's `FakeLag`, whose delay engine is a shared request/handler/timeout subsystem; here each module owns its queue outright, the convention the rest of the addon already runs on. Connection-keeping packets (keep-alives, pings, chunk-batch traffic, bundles) always pass through untouched, so the hold cannot starve the world or read as a dying connection. The cost is stated in the description: released bursts read as timer anomalies on servers that count packets.

New network module `lag-range`: the same hold, but conditional - engaged only while closing on a target inside the reach band, or right after a hit landed inside the three-block minimum, and flushed the moment the exchange changes shape: a hit of your own, taking damage, a sprint restart, raising your sword, throwing a splash, opening a screen, the target leaving the band. Ported from Raven B4's `LagRange` with the engage shape intact; the 1.8 hurt-window hit-marking and the first-person indicator are not carried over, and the closest target scan replaces the original's targeting helper.

New network module `backtrack`: holds one target's movement packets while the withheld position is the better one to swing at - further along your aim ray than the position this client still shows, inside the reach band, on the stale side of the exchange - and releases them by age, damage, teleport or target change. The geometry lives in `BacktrackMath` (ray/box entry distance, the hold decision table), unit tested in `BacktrackMathTest` including the border-grown box edge cases. Ported from Raven B4's `Backtrack` with three deliberate deviations: the hold is scoped to one entity's movement packets rather than everything-but-a-whitelist (a held session cannot starve the world of chunks), the 1.8 ghost rendering is dropped, and the release clock is wall-clock milliseconds rather than tick counts. Against a lag-compensating server the effect is bounded by what it already grants; the description says so.

New combat module `rod-aimbot`: a right click with an uncast rod is intercepted, the closest valid player inside the cone is picked, and the cast is staged against where they will be when the hook arrives - `predicted-ticks` projects their observed motion through vanilla's own per-tick constants (air drag 0.91, gravity 0.08 with 0.98 drag, ground friction 0.546). Ported from Raven B4's `RodAimbot` with the same gates (cone, distance, invisibility, bots, teammates) and its deviations stated: the camera is never taken - the cast rotation is spoofed server-side through `PreRotate`, so the interaction departs before the movement packet from a rotation the server acknowledged, and the aim keeps refreshing every tick until the cast lands rather than only when the original's motion event fires. Both rotation axes are snapped onto the sensitivity grid with the 7.18.4 machinery - a cast angle no mouse could produce is exactly what the rotation checks read. The reel-in is deliberately left to the player: the hook is where it is, and a second interception would fight the hand that cast it. The projection and the angle conventions live in `EntityPredict` and `RodAimMath`, unit tested in `RodAimMathTest` (fall and friction shapes, yaw/pitch conventions, cone wrap).

Fixed the quit hang. Clicking Quit used to freeze the client for twenty seconds and end in a `ClientShutdownWatchdog` crash report with exit code -8. The cause: Baritone's cache workers are non-daemon threads parked forever in a `LinkedBlockingQueue.take()` inside a loop that catches `InterruptedException` and `Throwable` and keeps parking - so neither an interrupt nor a `shutdownNow()` can release a worker that is already parked there, and once `main()` returns the JVM waits on them until vanilla's watchdog force-kills the process. The fix is a shutdown reaper: a daemon thread started at addon init that watches the main thread, and the moment `main()` has returned invokes `System.exit(0)` - shutdown hooks run, the halt takes the parked threads with it, and quitting is clean and immediate. When every thread is well behaved the natural shutdown wins the race and the forced exit is a no-op on an already-halting JVM. Covered by `ShutdownReaperTest` (fires on death, stays quiet while watched, daemon by construction).

Removed fourteen dead modules after grading every one of them against the 26.2 server model. Twelve were 1.8-era packet relics that cannot function against a server-side simulation and only ever produced flags: `more-carry` (crafting-slot carry - servers repopulate containers on close), `bungeecord-spoof` (forwarding data is proxy-side; a client injection just fingerprints), `kick` (ESC menu exists), `portal-exploits` (with its two serving mixins, `NetherPortalBlockMixin` and `ScreenMixin`), `reset-vl` (modern anticheats do not keep reloggable violation levels), `sleep-walker` (the server ejects a moving sleeper), `chorus-exploit` (the teleport is server-authoritative), `v-click-tp` (client setPos rubber-bands without permission), `vehicle-one-hit` (vehicle health is server-side), `v-ghost-hand` (server raycasts), `time-shift` and `v-anti-hunger`. The other two were worse than dead: the repo's own `OrphanModuleTest` audit had already established that `text-field-protect`, `extended-firework` and `v-ghost-hand` were wired to nothing - their advertised features never ran because the mixins they waited on were never written - so those settings took space in the GUI while doing literally nothing. The orphan and inert allowlists are empty now, and the drift assertions keep them that way.

Fixed V Scaffold sending pitch steps no mouse can produce. The shared `RotationGcd` grid was verified against the 26.2 client bytecode and is correct: `MouseHandler.turnPlayer` multiplies mouse counts by `f³ × 8` and `Entity.turn` scales that by `0.15`, so the real grid step is `f³ × 1.2` - exactly what the utility computes, and exactly what the network interceptor's duplicate of the formula computes. The scaffold was the fault: it imported the utility and never called it, so the staged pitch went out as the raw `smoothed + wobble` float, and the delta between consecutive rotations - the thing Grim's `RotationPlace` reachability test actually validates - landed between the grid lines (the session's two `RotationPlace` flags). The pitch handed to the server is now snapped onto the grid at both staging sites, measured from the rotation the server already holds, since what is validated is the step, not the absolute angle. The yaw is deliberately untouched: it is the camera's own, so its step is a real mouse turn by construction.

The snap never rounds a requested movement away. The pitch wobble is smaller than one grid step at most sensitivities, and a naive round-to-nearest would erase it, leaving the rotation repeating exactly - the fingerprint the wobble exists to avoid (`AimDuplicateLook`). A real but sub-grid step now becomes one whole grid step in the requested direction, the smallest movement a real mouse can make; a genuinely zero step still invents nothing. The smoothing and wobble constructs are untouched - the grid is applied where the aim is handed to Meteor, in the new `RotationGcd.quantizeFrom`, covered by four new `RotationGcdTest` cases: relative snapping, the sub-grid bump, two hundred ticks of hold oscillation staying on-grid and near the aim, and degenerate sensitivities passing the target through unchanged.

The Simulation flag wall from the same session is not explained by anything this codebase writes: the scaffold's whole path was checked and there is not a single velocity write in it - the module stages rotations and clicks, and applies no motion of its own. The steady `.054600` repeat is one 0.1/tick step of velocity re-injected and ground-frictioned (0.6 × 0.91) every tick, which is a physics-versus-prediction mismatch, not a motion hack. Retest on Grim after this build; if the rotation-side flags are gone and Simulation remains, the next suspect is the just-placed-block confirmation window, isolable with a live A/B - module on while standing still, then while walking, then while bridging.

Debug round: a head-to-head reread of the 7.18.x additions against their sources - the pause masks, the damage and knockback bookkeeping, the state resets, the registration and the version sync - shipping the fixes the reread found. Three real ones:

Fixed `latency-alerts` limbo carve-out losing half of the original's test: Raven's limbo is The End dimension AND an empty scoreboard sidebar, and the port had kept only the dimension half, so the module went silent inside any The End world - actually hiding genuine packet-loss alerts in minigames played there. Now the exact conjunction in `inLimbo()`: the `DisplaySlot.SIDEBAR` objective absent, or present with zero scored rows, and the dimension The End.

Fixed `latency-alerts` first-alert timing: the original zeroes its last-alert stamp on disable and stamps only the packet clock on enable, so the first stall raises at the earliest legal moment; the port's reset-both-on-activate delayed every first alert by a full alert interval after toggling. Enable and disable mirror the original now, and the disable and no-player legs clear the last-packet name the way the original's branches do.

Fixed two `hit-select` parity breaks: the tick clock is cleared on enable (the original does; the wait-first window measures exchange age, not addon uptime), and `item-blacklist` is now hidden until `filter-blacklisted-items` is on - the original's guiUpdate behavior, riding the addon's existing `.visible` precedent. `missed-swings-cancel-rate`'s description now tells the truth about the packet level: it filters attack packets on non-player entities, and air swings are out of reach there because vanilla never sends an attack packet for an empty crosshair - Raven's 1.8 build could intercept them, a packet filter cannot.

Reread, no fault found everywhere else: `hit-select`'s pause/mask/criticals logic matches the original step-for-step (including the strict pause release clock and the raw-mask write on server confirmation), `jump-reset`, `no-jump-delay` and `auto-requeue` hold their shapes and their state resets, the `noJumpDelay` accessor targets the javap-verified field, and `ItemListSetting`'s builder seeds a non-null empty-list default (bytecode-checked), so building `item-blacklist` without `defaultValue` was already safe. The skipped suite member is `BuildScriptsTest`'s `@DisabledOnOs(WINDOWS)` case, idle on this machine on purpose.

New combat module `hit-select`: filters clicks the server would ignore anyway - a hit that lands inside a target's invulnerability window is voided by every server, while the click still spends the attacker's weapon cooldown and the momentum of the exchange. Ported from Raven B4's `HitSelect` with its decision extracted into `HitSelectRules` (bursts predicted from the attacker's own hit, the optional server-timing gate, the sticky pause holding any block reason for its duration, the wait-for-first-hit hold, the criticals gate, the three-block reach, the percent cancel rates), with unit tests in `HitSelectRulesTest`. Two ports findings shipped with the port: Raven's hurt-window sync and its `maxHurtTime` fallback are unwired in the original - the live path only ever starts ten-tick windows from a passed hit, which is what the port keeps and every one of them is exclusive-end-tested; and 26.2 gives attacks their own `ServerboundAttackPacket`, so the filter runs there and the rejected click's vanilla swing packet still leaves the client - the visible behaviour Raven's "fake swing" option bought, without the option. The mouse-over-first/else-closest target precedence and the eye-to-nearest-box-face reach are Raven's own; Raven's friends list and bot list carve-outs have no equivalent here and are dropped; `ignore-teammates` rides on vanilla `isAlliedTo`; weapon detection rides on the repo's `McCompat.isWeapon` (the same check the other combat modules hold to), since 26.2 swords carry a weapon data component instead of a `SwordItem` class and there is no sword class to instanceof.

New misc module `latency-alerts`: the gap since the last packet the server sent is measured every tick, and once it crosses the `high-latency` threshold an alert prints with the gap and the last packet seen - at most once per `alert-interval` so a stall does not flood the chat. Ported from Raven B4's `LatencyAlerts` with the same measurement, interval guard and its limbo carve-out (measured the same way, on The End dimension); the hover component it hung the details on is replaced by the details printed inline.

Graded-and-rejected for this increment: larpclient's `HoverTotem` (already inside `auto-inv-totem` - it ships the "merged with HoverTotem" description) and Raven's `HitBox` (needs a pick-interception mixin at the current `GameRendererMixin`'s cost, for a reach that Grim's player-attack-range check refuses to honour beyond three blocks anyway).

New movement module `no-jump-delay`: the vanilla jump cooldown (`LivingEntity.noJumpDelay`, ticked down from ten after every jump) is clamped each tick to the `jump-delay` setting, so the default of 0 lets the jump be taken again the grounded tick after the last one. The port clamps instead of writing zero a decision the 26.2-era source it was transcribed from got right: a constant zero would defeat the countdown itself, and a jump would never be allowed again. The field is reached through a new `LivingEntityAccessor` mixin (the addon's first accessor into an entity class, registered in `venomous.mixins.json`).

New misc module `auto-requeue`: runs the command behind a game's play-again chat button, held until the `delay` has passed. Ported from Raven B4's `AutoRequeue` with its shape kept - a message whose text matches the `trigger-text` is scanned for a command click event, the command is held until it is run, and a fresh world join discards what was held, because requeueing belongs to the game the message was sent in. Two deliberate deviations: Raven matched the server's own button wording ("Click here"), where the port takes the first run-command click event wherever it sits in the component tree and matches the trigger text somewhat; and Raven routed the click value through 1.8.9's single send method, where the port splits on the leading slash - `sendCommand` for a `/queue`, `sendChat` otherwise.

Surveyed further archive ports for this increment and rejected them for cause: Raven's `AntiDebuff` is 1.8.9 render plumbing already covered by `anti-blind`; `InstantStop` and `NullMove` need an input-injection event Meteor does not expose (`PrePlayerInputEvent` is Raven-internal) for a small payoff; `StopMotion` zeroes vertical velocity mid-air, which is a predictable gravity mismatch on the servers this addon is tuned for; `KeepSprint`'s 1.8.9 logic is attack-slowdown math that does not exist in modern code, and its modern descendant is partially covered by `super-kb`'s W-TAP; larpclient's `PanicSlot` force-selects a hotbar slot. The bigger ports (`HitSelect`, the lag-queue trio, `Clutch`, `HitBox`) stay queued for their own increments.

New combat module `jump-reset`: pressing the jump key on the tick a hit lands, so the knockback multiplies into the jump and lands a fraction of its range. Ported from Raven B4's `JumpReset` module and its gate list, one boolean at a time: only a fresh growth of the hurt window counts as a hit (a drained window mid-combo is the same hit, not a new one), the player must be grounded ("a jump can only start from the ground"), the window may not be burning or jump-boost/poison/wither-tinted (`MobEffects` reads, Raven's own three), the movement direction must line up with the facing, and the three optional gates ship with Raven's defaults - attack key waived, walking-forward required, crosshair-on-player required.

The port keeps Raven's landing guard: hurt time that arrives while standing on ground after falling further than three blocks is the fall's own damage, not a hit, and is suppressed once. The one-tick press is Meteor-native: the module presses `keyJump` in `TickEvent.Pre` only when the player was not already holding it, and releases its own press before the next tick's decision, so the tap covers exactly one input window. The module only ever releases a press it made itself - the key mapping is shared with the game's own events, so an unconditional release would clobber a jump the player is holding.

Raven's knockback arc check is shipped honestly rather than copied: its `inFov(GetDirection, 330, ...)` halves its argument to a ±165 degree tolerance and therefore passes everything except a movement within fifteen degrees of exactly backwards - a no-op in practice. `JumpResetRules` carries the wrap-aware `withinArc` with the same full-arc semantics and the same 330 default behind the `motion-arc` setting (documented as such), so lowering it actually rejects sideways and rear hits; standing still on the hurt tick - before the knockback is applied - waives the gate instead of being judged against yaw zero. The decision lives in `JumpResetRules` (`motionYawOf` follows Minecraft's yaw convention: +Z is 0, +X is -90) with unit tests in `JumpResetRulesTest`; every new setting is read.

`v-scaffold` keeps the rotation the server is told on the camera's own yaw across every tick of a bridging run, not only on the ticks the staging loop had a target to aim at. Meteor consumes each rotation it is handed in the same tick, but it also keeps the last one and re-sends it for up to `rotation-hold` ticks (default 4) whenever no fresh rotation is staged - writing the player's own rotation to that staged angle for the length of each packet, while the position delta in those packets was integrated by physics that ran on the live camera. Every degree the mouse moved since the staging is therefore a walk the server did not predict, and Grim's `Simulation` reports it: the 7.17.1 run collected 119 one-millimetre-scale flags in exactly that shape - decaying clusters that restarted with each staging gap. The gap came from the ticks that early-return out of every loop (no supporting face for the cell mid-jump, no block in the hotbar, no cell underfoot), which are precisely the ticks that skipped `Rotations.rotate()`. `PreRotate.followCameraYaw` now re-stages the rotation on those ticks - from each no-target return in `tickGrim`, `tickStandardMode` and `aimAndPlace` - with the camera's yaw read fresh that tick, the held aim pitch (`stagedPitch`) and its wobble, pending an aim within a one-second linger of the last staging. The queue is untouched, the age-out clock keeps running, nothing is written to the camera, there is no new setting, and the crouch is unchanged.

`PreRotate.isServerReady` now honours the `yawMatters` flag it already records, whose documented contract ("the action waits only for the pitch to be sent") was silently ignored - a moving mouse held every placement back a tick, and a staged rotation was judged against a frozen staging yaw with a 1.5 degree tolerance, which is exactly the mouse being measured rather than the rotation. The readiness decision now lives in `RotationReadiness` (yaw comparison wraps around the 0/360 seam, tolerance inclusive on both axes) with unit tests (`RotationReadinessTest`, `CameraFollowTest`, and `find` coverage in `DeferredActionsTest`).

Ported two timing ideas from Raven B4's scaffold, with the derivations behind each, to `v-scaffold`: wall-clock time since the last placement before it presses, instead of squeezing the edge crouch back on the tick after a placement leaves. Holding is not pressing — an already-down key is left alone — and releases are never delayed, because a crouch held past its point is a walking-into-air bug. Together with `SneakTiming` this turns the sneak-toggle cadence from one toggle per placement into bursts at the places a real hand would squeeze the crouch. performed the last placement — 710ms while sprinting, 110ms while walking, 460ms idle, Raven's numbers — instead of drifting along with the walk between placements. A staged placement turns the hold off entirely, because that is when the server's ray has to reach the face; the pitch wobble keeps running either way so the rotation never repeats exactly for `AimDuplicateLook`.

Fixed `v-scaffold` placing on POST — the anticheat named it directly: `Looks like you are currently attacking/placing on POST, this is a very common check on most anti-cheats`. Meteor's `BlockUtils.place(..., rotate = true, ...)` calls `Rotations.rotate(yaw, pitch, runnable)`, whose callback Meteor runs from `SendMovementPacketsEvent.Post`, so the interaction left *after* the movement packet. Only GrimScaffold and NCP were routed through `PreRotate`; every other path passed `rotate = true` straight to `BlockUtils`. Rotation-and-place is now always `aimAndPlace`, and the rotating `place(pos, shouldRotate)` overload has been deleted so no call site can reintroduce it.

Removed the `expand`, `vulcan-expand` and `vulcan-sprint` techniques from `v-scaffold`, along with the `Expand` and `Vulcan` setting groups and every setting that belonged to them. They placed extra blocks per tick, which no placement cadence survives and which the anticheat's straight-line minimum punishes hardest. Nine techniques remain: GrimScaffold, AutoSneak, BridgeMacro, VapeBridge, NCPNormal and Normal.

Added activity guards across the combat modules, ported from a decompile of Vape v4.10. Each one stops the client doing something a person would not: `aimbot` gained `click-aim` (only aim while the attack key is held), `check-block-break` (do not aim while mining) and `limit-to-items` — the first two close a real inconsistency, because `auto-clicker-plus` already refused to click unless the attack key was down while the aimer tracked anyone unconditionally. `auto-clicker-plus` gained `require-entity`, since nothing stopped it firing on empty air. `velocity-plus` gained `chance`, `water-check` and `only-when-targeting`; reducing every knockback in every situation is itself a pattern. `v-scaffold` gained `block-whitelist`/`block-blacklist` and `pitch-check`/ `pitch-threshold`. All default to off or permissive so existing behaviour is unchanged.

Removed the `god-bridge` and `breezily` techniques from `v-scaffold`. Both drove the camera directly, which is the behaviour this release exists to undo: `god-bridge` jumped, looked back and down, placed beneath the jump and eased the view forward again, while `breezily` pulsed the player sideways at the edge and placed on each pulse. Neither survived a real bridge. Removing them took out the last callers of the camera slew, so `smoothAimAt`, `smoothViewTo`, `applyLook`, `aimNoise`, the per-axis aim velocities, `CAPTURE_DEGREES`, and the `AimEase`/`RotationGcd` imports went with them — all of which existed only to write a GCD-quantised look change to the camera, and none of which is reachable now that nothing drives the view. `v-scaffold` is down 127 lines.

`v-scaffold` no longer snaps out of its crouch the instant a bridge edge clears. All four auto-sneak sites were a bare `if (edge) crouch(); else stand();`, so the crouch came up 50ms after it went down. That is the exact shape AntiCheat-Addition's `Scaffold.parts.Safewalk.Timing` flags for 20 VL — moved within 355ms, stopped within 175ms, and not held sneaking for more than 148ms — and it is also simply how a human does not move, since nobody lands on a new block and stands straight back up. The crouch is now held for a configurable `sneak-delay` (default 200ms, the middle of Vape's 100/200/500 presets) with a 30ms floor so a one-tick edge blip cannot produce a zero-length crouch. The decision lives in the pure, unit-tested `SneakTiming`. GodBridge and Breezily manage their own crouch phase-by-phase and were left alone deliberately.

Removed the last GitHub references now that the project lives on GitLab. `fabric.mod.json`'s `contact.sources` pointed at a dead `github.com` repository, and `VenomousAddon.getRepo()` still declared one — Meteor's addon API can only describe GitHub (`GithubRepo` is a `final record` with no host field), so the honest value is `null`, which is Meteor's own default and is null-checked before use. The cost is that the title screen no longer offers a commit link; `contact.sources` is now the only source pointer and points at the GitLab group. The credited author is derived from that URL rather than hardcoded, so the two cannot drift apart again.

Corrected the mod's credited author. `fabric.mod.json` still named a personal handle while the repository and the changelog had both moved to International Duck Incorporated, so anything reading the mod listing was told the wrong owner. The two are now asserted to agree, against the packaged resource rather than the source file, so the shipped jar is what gets checked.

Fixed `v-scaffold`'s default placement cadence being detectable on its own, independent of rotation. AntiCheat-Addition's `ScaffoldAverageBatchProcessor` averages the real gaps between placements on one straight line and flags anything faster than its `placement_delay` default of 238ms, and a straight bridge is the *strict* case — diagonal building is allowed 138ms. The default `place-delay` of 3 produced `3 + random(0..2)` ticks, a 200ms mean, so it was under the floor by construction. Observed on AntiCheat-Addition as `failed scaffold x15` then `x20`; decoding its `1.1 * (238 - actual) + 5` puts the measured average at ~229ms and ~224ms, which is the 200ms nominal plus tick scheduling. The default is now 5 and the invariant lives in the pure, unit-tested `ScaffoldCadence` so the setting and its guard cannot drift apart.

`v-scaffold` no longer drags the player's view onto the server's rotation. Both the GrimScaffold and the NCP placement paths snapped the camera to whatever the block needed, so bridging overrode where you were looking and the mouse fought the client. They now hand the rotation to Meteor and defer the placement to `SendMovementPacketsEvent.Pre` through `PreRotate`, so the server is aimed correctly while your camera stays exactly where you put it. The `rotate` setting gates both paths; with it off, placement happens immediately as before. GodBridge still drives the camera deliberately — looking back and down is the whole point of that mode.

Fixed `v-scaffold` sweeping absurdly slowly, and only in one direction. `AimEase.step` treats velocity as a magnitude, but `nextVelocity` handed back the *signed* step. A leftward sweep therefore compared a negative velocity against a positive target and the acceleration ramp collapsed, crawling toward the ceiling instead of reaching it. Rightward sweeps looked correct, which is why this read as a general sluggishness rather than a sign bug. `nextVelocity` now returns `Math.abs(step(...))`.

Fixed the startup banner advertising the wrong version. `VenomousAddon.VERSION` was maintained by hand while the build numbered the jar from `libs.versions.toml`, so 7.0.1 shipped printing `V7.0.0`. The two are now asserted equal, the version may be written down exactly once in the addon class, and the banner reads the constant. `AddonMetadataTest` fails the build otherwise.

Reindented the recovered sources from 3-space to 4-space, matching the hand-written files. The recovered tree carried Vineflower's 3-space output, so 122 of 150 Java files were formatted differently from the rest; the change is whitespace-only and leaves compiled output byte-identical.

Moved `ServerAnalyzer` from `modules/detection` to `utils`. It is a helper owned by `AntiCheatDetect` rather than a registrable module, so `modules/` now contains only modules and the registry tests no longer need to special-case it.

Narrowed `ServerAnalyzer.getServerIp`'s undocumented `catch (Throwable)` to `catch (LinkageError)` and documented why: `MeteorClient`'s static initialiser throws `ExceptionInInitializerError` outside a running game, which is an `Error`, so a `RuntimeException` catch silently stops covering it. Genuine `Error`s now propagate.
`v-ghost-hand` no longer leaves Meteor's `StorageESP` running forever after it is switched off, and now only disables an ESP it enabled itself.
`pearl-wind-macro` no longer fires its queued rotation actions after being disabled, which threw items at stale hotbar slots from an inactive module.

Implemented the advertised humanlike timing in `middle-click-action`. Its `technique`, `min-cps` and `max-cps` settings were decorative — the module acted instantly on the middle-click down-edge and never read them. Timing now lives in the pure, unit-tested `ClickTiming` helper, and the target is resolved on the press so the delay cannot act on a different entity than the one clicked.

Every `PreRotate` consumer kept running its deferred action after being switched off, because nothing re-checked that the action was still wanted. `PreRotate` now takes a mandatory guard — `rotateThen(this, …)` for modules, or any `Guard` for non-modules — and the unguarded overloads are gone, so the compiler enforces it.

`v-auto-city` and `auto-break-selected` captured a mutable field in their deferred action, so the rotation was computed for one block while the action ran against another. Both now capture the target by value. `auto-break-selected` additionally dereferenced a target that its own `resetMining()` teardown had just nulled, which could throw.

Deferred actions no longer pile up. A module that re-requested its action every tick while the rotation was settling queued one entry per tick, and every copy fired in the same tick once the rotation landed — repeated `START`/`STOP` destroy packets for a single block. Queueing now supersedes the caller's own earlier entry, expressing current intent instead of a backlog.

Fixed ready actions running in reverse queue order. They were collected back-to-front so entries could be removed while iterating, and were never put back in order. A macro queuing two actions on one aim would have run them backwards.
Added `PreRotate.rotateThenSequence` for macros that must run every step, such as `pearl-wind-macro` throwing an item and then using a charge on the same aim.

Made `v-scaffold` actually human-shaped. Its camera moved at a fixed 7°/tick for the whole sweep and stopped dead on the target, which no hand produces; edge thresholds fired at identical distances every time; and placements landed exactly `place-delay` ticks apart, forever. Aim now eases in, decelerates into the target and carries per-tick noise, thresholds and cadence are jittered, and — most importantly — rotation deltas are quantised to the sensitivity GCD grid. A real mouse emits only whole multiples of that grid, so the old unquantised `setYRot` sweep produced angles no human could generate. That is what `Aimbot` and `KillAura` already did via their `gcd-fix` settings; scaffold had neither.

Extracted the sensitivity GCD formula into `RotationGcd` and the easing curve into `AimEase`, both free of Minecraft types so they unit-test on a plain JVM. The GCD formula had been copy-pasted into `Aimbot`, `KillAura` and `GlobalNetworkInterceptor`.

Implemented fifteen settings that were registered in the GUI but never read, so they silently did nothing. `invis-esp` passed a hardcoded `0` for line width; `no-fall-plus` never consulted `grim-save-ticks`; `new-chunks` only ever rendered the new-chunk colour; `auto-ez` tracked a streak it never reported; `teams` ignored `armor-color`; `tickbase` banked a burst while idle regardless of `only-on-attack`; `targetlock` never checked `combat-only`; `lethality` ignored `hurt-time-check`; `autochatgame` had no unscramble solver at all despite detecting the game type; `v-blink`'s `dummy` setting had no renderer behind it.
Removed `skeleton-esp`'s `line-width` setting instead of implementing it: `Renderer3D.line` takes no width argument, so there is no call that could honour it.

Removed dead code in `auto-farm`: `rotateTo`, `isLookingAt` and `wrapDegrees` had no callers. `rotateTo` was a verbatim copy of the constant-rate, un-quantised rotation logic just removed from scaffold, so leaving it in place invited that bug being reintroduced.
Added `DeadSettingTest`, which fails the build if a module registers a setting it never reads. It carries a self-test asserting the detector can still fire.

Wrote the four modules that were settings-only shells, and gave each real behaviour. teleport request, distinguished from ordinary position packets by a grace window around outbound accept-teleport packets. Reports session and recent counts. server-acceptable position increments and returning afterwards, with optional eased, GCD-quantised camera rotation. nearest player in range.

**Plug-and-play module folder.** `.java` files below `config/champions-mod/modules/` are now compiled and registered automatically, so a drop-in module needs no hash confirmation, no `java modules reload`, and no console command at all. Recursive drop-folder hardening: module sources are recognised at any depth, dot-files and dot-directories (including the generated `.build/` folder, editor scratch files such as `.Module.java.swp`, and `Module.java~` backups) are ignored everywhere, and a short `README.txt` explaining the rules is written into the folder the first time it is created.

Change detection that stays quiet: a metadata fingerprint of the folder is polled once a second, a change is only acted on after a short settled period so a staged file save is one reload, and a folder state that failed to compile is left alone until the files change so compiler errors print once instead of every second.

**Works against current Beacon again.** Bagley now builds against Beacon `2.0.0-prerelease` (the current `main`, including the new Chromium web UI and onboarding work) as well as `1.9.0`. No addon API used by Bagley changed between the two, so no module code was touched.

**Fixed the build failure that broke CI.** Beacon's published POM advertises its own bundled runtime libraries - the MCEF Chromium bridge (`net.ccbluex:mcef`, published only on `maven.ccbluex.net`), OkHttp and Kotlin - so resolving `net.beacon:beacon-<mc>:<version>` pulled in artifacts Bagley has no repository for and every Gradle configuration failed with `Could not find net.ccbluex:mcef:...`. The Beacon API is now consumed as a non-transitive `compileOnly` dependency: addons compile against Beacon's classes only, and Fabric Loader supplies Beacon's nested libraries at runtime from the installed Beacon jar.

**`BEACON_REF` and the Beacon version can no longer drift.** CI used to clone Beacon `main` and publish it to Maven Local while `gradle.properties` still pinned `beacon_version=1.9.0`, so the build only worked as long as the ref happened to be that release. The pipeline now reads `mod_version` out of the Beacon checkout it just cloned and exports it as `BEACON_VERSION`, so whichever Beacon ref is selected, the artifact Bagley compiles against is the one that checkout produced. `beacon_version` stays as the local-development default and is `2.0.0-prerelease`.
Accepts Beacon `>=1.9.0 <3.0.0` at runtime (`fabric.mod.json`), so the current `2.0.0-prerelease` builds and the next 2.x releases load instead of being rejected by the old `<2.0.0` range.

Documented that Beacon does not publish its API to the Maven package registry yet, so builds resolve it from Maven Local or `-Pbeacon_api_jar`; the README previously pointed at a registry copy that does not exist.
